beliefs.practice: Require a tenantId equality predicate on every read/write operation and enforce it centrally (e.g., a Mongoose repository-layer plugin that injects { tenantId } into queries and rejects any operation that would run without it).

Create and maintain compound indexes with tenantId as the leading key: at minimum (tenantId ASC, sku ASC) and (tenantId ASC, createdAt DESC); create indexes idempotently during deployment/seed and verify they exist at startup.
Enforce uniqueness for tenant-scoped unique fields using a compound unique index (e.g., unique index on (tenantId, sku)) rather than a global unique constraint.

Read the cluster connection string from environment or a secrets store at runtime (do not commit credentials to repo); in production use Azure Key Vault or managed identity-based secrets instead of plain env vars.
Require TLS/SSL for all client connections (enable tls/ssl in connection options and reject insecure connections); do not disable certificate verification in production.

Reuse a single shared Mongoose/MongoDB driver connection pool for the app and tune maxPoolSize (maxPoolSize / connection pool size) to match expected concurrency; do not open a new connection per request.

Honor server 'Retry-After' and implement exponential backoff for transient errors and 429 (Request Rate Too Large) throttling; treat 429 as retryable with backoff and monitor RU usage to reduce throttles.

Provision throughput (RU/s) appropriately: either database-level or collection-level throughput, consider autoscale/elastic to handle spikes, and size RU to expected read/write patterns to avoid 429s.

Design queries to use the tenantId-leading compound indexes: include tenantId equality in filters, avoid filtering on non-indexed fields, and when sorting on createdAt use the (tenantId, createdAt) index to avoid in-memory sorts.

Create indexes in an idempotent, off-peak manner (or as part of deployment) and avoid building large indexes synchronously on a production cluster during heavy traffic; prefer background/build-on-deploy patterns.
Use projection to return only required fields and use Mongoose's lean() for high-throughput read paths to reduce memory/cpu overhead of hydration.
Do not rely on multi-document transactions for normal tenant-scoped operations; favor single-document atomic updates or embed related data where possible to avoid transaction overhead and RU cost.
Monitor query plans and index usage with explain(), database profiler and Azure metrics; remove unused indexes that consume RU and storage and tune indexes to real query patterns.
Handle large result sets with pagination (skip/limit or better, range/seek-based pagination keyed by (tenantId, createdAt) using the compound index) rather than fetching and sorting all rows.

For vector search, store vectors in a fixed-dimension numeric array field, create a vector index with explicit algorithm parameters (e.g., HNSW M and efConstruction or IVF parameters) and choose metric (cosine / euclidean) that matches similarity semantics; ensure index parameters are tuned for cardinality and dimensionality.

Respect the server's supported MongoDB wire protocol version and server features: avoid relying on MongoDB-server features not supported by Cosmos/Mongo API (confirm support for retryable writes, transactions, aggregation stages you use), and fall back if a feature is unsupported.
Keep documents reasonably small (avoid very large embedded arrays/blobs); target under MongoDB's BSON limit (~16MB) and be conservative to reduce RU cost and network transfer size.
Do not log sensitive fields such as connection strings, primary keys, or tenant secrets; mask or redact sensitive values in logs and error messages.

Detect and block dangerous repository operations (e.g., updateMany, deleteMany without tenantId) via code review or automated tests; include unit/integration tests that assert tenant isolation (queries cannot return results from other tenantIds).

Make seeding scripts idempotent and safe to run repeatedly against the same database (check for existing docs/indexes before inserting/creating), and avoid changing user/production data when running developer seeds.

Plan for backups/restore: rely on Azure Cosmos DB automatic backups for point-in-time recovery where available, but also provide export/import tooling (JSON/backup) for long-term archival or cross-region recovery.

When creating schema-like Mongoose models for a polyglot, shared-collection multi-tenant design, avoid storing too many nullable fields; prefer small, typed fields and use discriminators or a type field for different document shapes to keep index selectivity predictable.
